Name: Angie Muse
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

I did work several years ago with a teacher in my school. I was her instructional coach. All of my teachers received the layered reading and writing training. I helped to give that training--though it was source-based argument work, and went beyond the work of this module. I had taken the training earlier and helped present this training to my teachers.

Recently, I also did a 1/2 day training session with teachers in the Rockwood school district. We took them through this process.

In both instances, teachers experienced a paradigm shift, as did I. Academic writing is a process of reading, talking, and writing. It is an organic, slippery thing that cannot be fully regimented. We needed to get used to the messiness of real writring.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
Fromt the work I did with teachers in my school, the thing that sticks with me is not only the pride of the students--whose work was meaningful because of the mental investment--but also the pride of the teacher who also invested a lot. At first, she focused on the things students didn't do in the paper. But, when she focused on what they COULD do, her perspective shifted.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? What aspects of your students’ writing are you most curious to explore more deeply with colleagues during our April regroup? What, if any, questions do you h:
Well, I didn't do this reflection before the April regroup, but I came to that meeting wanted to hear what teachers thought about the UST tool. In my recent work with Rockwood teachers, I heard sevearl complaints that the UST didn't get to aspects of writing that were important (like grammar). I guess we didn't do a good job of training them on the focus of the UST!!! Anyway, I know that teachers are used to scoring final product writing on a range of skills, and that using a UST to give feedback on specific skills was a new thing for most people. So, I was curious to see their thoughts about the tool.
